facts.raw_span: intractable mucocutaneous lesions that had been evolving for 10 years
No swollen cervical and axillary lymph nodes were palpable
Small bullae, erosions, and crusts were present on the lower lip
Erosions with epithelized mucosa were observed in the oral cavity
Flaccid discrete and coalesced bullae, crusts, and erosions over erythematous and cicatricial lesions were present on the face, trunk, and extremities
Chest, abdomen, and pelvic computed tomography showed no abnormalities
Gastrointestinal endoscopy and colonoscopy results identified no abnormalities
Skin biopsy revealed spongiosis and numerous neutrophils with nuclear dust in the epidermis and superficial perivascular dermatitis with predominant infiltration of lymphocytes in the dermis
No obvious deposits of IgG, IgA, and C3 to either the epithelial cell surface or the basement membrane zone
Positive for IgG autoantibodies to envoplakin (210 kDa) and periplakin (190 kDa)
Negative for Dsg1, Dsg3, and BP180 16th noncollagenous domain
Negative for BP230, type VII collagen, and desmocollins 1 to 3

concepts.why: The presence of autoantibodies to envoplakin and periplakin, as well as the clinical findings of mucocutaneous lesions, suggest paraneoplastic pemphigus.
The clinical findings of flaccid bullae, erosions, and crusts on the skin and mucous membranes are consistent with pemphigus vulgaris.
The presence of superficial perivascular dermatitis and the absence of deposits of IgG, IgA, and C3 suggest bullous pemphigoid.
The clinical findings of mucocutaneous lesions and the presence of autoantibodies to type VII collagen suggest epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.
The presence of linear deposits of IgA at the basement membrane zone and the clinical findings of mucocutaneous lesions suggest linear IgA bullous dermatosis.
The clinical findings of mucocutaneous lesions and the presence of autoantibodies to BP180 suggest mucous membrane pemphigoid.
The presence of autoantibodies to envoplakin and periplakin, as well as the clinical findings of mucocutaneous lesions, suggest an autoimmune bullous disease.
The presence of superficial perivascular dermatitis and the absence of deposits of IgG, IgA, and C3 suggest dermatitis herpetiformis.
The presence of autoantibodies to envoplakin and periplakin, as well as the clinical findings of mucocutaneous lesions, suggest bullous lupus erythematosus.
The clinical findings of flaccid bullae, erosions, and crusts on the skin and mucous membranes are consistent with pemphigus foliaceus.
